title: Using AI to create maths resources in July 2025
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton revisits his 2024 experiments with AI chatbots, which stumbled over poor images and dubious maths, and reports that nine months later the tools produce resources that exceed his expectations. He sets out the foundational method he follows: a five-part prompt (context, topic, constraints, output format, examples), output requested in LaTeX, and compiling it free in Overleaf for a clean PDF. He walks through building a 20-question perimeter worksheet, stressing that the first draft is never right and that iterating with precise feedback also sharpens the prompt for reuse. He then asks whether this is good for teacher development, comparing it with using centrally planned resources and writing from scratch, and concludes that the benefit depends on whether the teacher thinks through the output or just accepts it. He ends candidly unsure whether a novice would learn as much as he does with twenty years of experience.
points: A reusable five-part prompt structure (context, topic, constraints, output format, examples) lets a teacher generate worksheets on any topic by changing only the topic line.
Asking for LaTeX and compiling it in Overleaf gives free, properly typeset worksheets and opens the door to diagrams that earlier chatbots could not produce.
Iterating with precise feedback on the output, and then refining the prompt, is where both better resources and teacher learning come from.
Barton applies his own cognitive-outsourcing argument about homework to teachers: AI-made resources teach little if accepted uncritically, much if engaged with.
He openly questions whether his enthusiasm depends on his two decades of expertise and whether novices would gain the same.
quotes: Long-time readers may remember that in October 2024, I experimented using AI to identify misconceptions, write diagnostic questions, and plan lessons. The results were mixed.
One thing you can be sure of is that the first output will not be exactly what you want.
But ultimately, the AI can only output based on our inputs, and 90% of the time, I find the fault lies with me not being as clear as I could be with my requirements.
We are now free to continue refining this set of questions in any way we want. We could ask for more questions or fewer questions, easier questions or harder questions.

If the teacher uses both the prompt and the first output without thought, they will learn little. However, if they work through the output and engage in a back-and-forth process, they may learn a great deal.
I believe I am learning a great deal by interacting with AI. I enjoy crafting the prompt to achieve the best possible first output.
But, is this only true because I can use my 20-year experience and (questionable!) expertise to engage with the AI in this way? Would a novice teacher enjoy the same benefits?
